title: Discovery Call vs Demo: When to Actually Demo (Framework)
summary: Discovery call vs demo: use this 3-signal framework to decide when to demo live, tease a preview, or wait, plus exact scripts, from Storylane Demo Suite.
body_markdown:
Here is my position on discovery call vs demo, and it will annoy people on both sides: when should you actually demo is not answered by a rule, it is answered by reading the call. "Always demo now" reps waste live time on features nobody asked about. "Never demo without full discovery" reps lose visual buyers who came to see the thing.


I am Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane, and the sequence is not the problem. The problem is that most reps decide when to demo before the call starts, then spend the call defending that decision.


This guide gives you a three-signal framework to decide in the moment, the exact scripts for each branch, and the mechanism that removes the tradeoff. It comes from how our own buyers describe getting this call right and wrong, so every rule here is one a real sales team already lives by.


## What's the Real Difference Between a Discovery Call and a Demo?


Most reps blur these two because they get booked as one meeting. A discovery call is a diagnosis. A demo is a prescription, and you cannot write a good prescription before the diagnosis is done.


### What a discovery call is for


Discovery exists to surface the buyer's real problem, its cost, and who else must agree before anything changes. Done well, it earns you the right to show something specific instead of touring the whole product. If you want the mechanics, we broke this down in[structuring your discovery process](https://www.storylane.io/blog/sales-discovery-process) .


### What a demo is for


A demo exists to make a diagnosed problem feel solved, on screen, for these people. The trap is treating it as a coverage exercise, and one solutions-engineering leader named exactly where that comes from.


> "part of our challenge is poor discovery on the front end leads to an SE, just, 'All right, well, I guess I'm going to demo the pro, like, the whole product.'"
>
>
> - \[Solutions Engineering manager, restaurant management software\]


The tell is comprehension loss: when a rep demos everything, the buyer stops tracking what matters. A demo also differs from a POC, which proves it works in your environment. If that trips up your buyers, point them to[how a demo differs from a POC](https://www.storylane.io/blog/major-differences-between-poc-and-demo) .


## Should You Ever Demo During a Discovery Call? The Short Answer


Yes, sometimes, and the people who say "never" are losing deals to buyers who came to see the product. The same leader called the current setup exactly what it is.


> "It's a weird broken system that we have in SaaS."
>
>
> - \[Solutions Engineering manager, restaurant management software\]


The fix is not to pick a side, it is to demo the right amount at the right moment. In practice that means a short, guided teaser tied to what you just heard, not a full walkthrough that buries the one thing they care about.


You keep discovery alive by asking questions between clicks instead of parking them all at the front. Here is the term this whole guide turns on.


> **Definition:** An interactive demo is a guided, click-through product experience you can show live or send as a leave-behind, built around a specific buyer's use case rather than a full product tour.


## The 3-Signal Framework: When to Demo Right Now vs. When to Wait


Every "should I demo now" decision comes down to three signals you can read inside the first ten minutes. Read them in order, and if the first two say go but the third says you are not ready, you tease instead of demo.


### Signal 1: What the buyer has explicitly asked for


If a buyer opens with "I'm here for the demo," that is data, not an obstacle. Visual buyers self-select into "show me now," and fighting it reads as evasive. So honor the ask, then earn two or three discovery answers inside the demo rather than before it.


### Signal 2: Deal complexity and stakeholder count


Not every deal deserves the same motion, and the buyers drew the line themselves. One SE leader saw a live interactive demo as overkill for a "10, 20, 30K deal" but essential in the enterprise range, where he described running 400, 500, and even two-million-dollar deals. Below that threshold, a guided leave-behind usually does more per hour.


### Signal 3: Whether you have a demo ready that's actually relevant to them


This is the signal reps skip. If the only thing you can show is a generic environment, demoing now is a gamble, and a principal SE captured the discipline instead.


> "We do so many things so well; if we're not prepared to show it right now, let's sideline that for another conversation."
>
>
> - \[principal sales engineer, restaurant management software\]


## Scenario-by-Scenario: What to Do in 6 Common Situations


Signals are principles, so here is what they look like across the six situations reps hit most. Read the signal column as the reason behind the action, not just a label.


The pattern to notice is that the explicit ask and your readiness usually decide the call faster than deal size does. Deal size is a tiebreaker, not the lead signal, which is why a $2M enterprise deal and a self-serve technical buyer land in different rows even though both are complex.


Take the inbound lead who clicked "get a demo" as a worked example. You open with a 60-second teaser on their likely use case, ask two discovery questions while it loads, then sideline anything you cannot show well for a follow-up. That single motion satisfies the ask, protects discovery, and sends them away with a guided leave-behind instead of an unwatched recording.


Use the table as a cheat sheet you can glance at while the call is still live.


Scenario Signal reading Action Why


Inbound lead who clicked a "get a demo" CTA Explicit ask is strong; intent is high Demo a short guided teaser on their likely use case, then backfill discovery They told you what they want; making them wait feels like a bait and switch


Cold outbound responder booking a first call No explicit ask; problem still unknown Run discovery first, tease at the end You have no diagnosis yet, so a demo would be a guess


Enterprise deal, multiple stakeholders on the call High complexity; high stakeholder count Discovery-led, then a tailored live demo or scheduled deep dive Several priorities in the room; a generic demo satisfies none of them


Technical buyer who wants to self-serve Wants control, not a guided tour Send a guided interactive demo as a leave-behind they can re-walk Guidance without a babysitter respects how they evaluate


Prospect who says "just show me a demo" up front Explicit ask is the whole opening Show a relevant teaser immediately, ask discovery questions between clicks Arguing for discovery first burns your credibility in minute one


Existing customer on a renewal or expansion call Context known; relevance is easy Demo the specific new capability tied to their current usage You already have the diagnosis, so skip to the prescription


## How to Structure a Combined Discovery-and-Demo Call


When the signals say demo on the same call, structure keeps it from collapsing into a full product tour. Run it in a fixed order so you never demo blind.


1. **Set the agenda in the first five minutes.** Name the two or three priorities you will cover and say plainly that anything outside them gets a follow-up. This is where you earn permission to sideline. Borrow the structure from[setting a demo agenda](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-agenda) , and pair it with a tight[discovery call agenda](https://www.storylane.io/blog/discovery-call-agenda) so neither half runs long.
2. **Ask your discovery questions before you show anything.** Even with a visual buyer, you can get two or three answers before the first click. Keep them tight and tied to what you plan to show, using[a discovery call script](https://www.storylane.io/blog/prepare-discovery-call-script) so you are not improvising.
3. **Transition into a teaser demo tied to what you just heard.** Pick the one workflow that maps to their top priority and show only that. The transition sentence matters, and I give you the exact words next.


The point of the order is restraint: you answer the one question you just diagnosed and defer the rest on purpose.


## Exact Talk Tracks: What to Say When a Prospect Demands a Demo Immediately


Everybody promises the script and then gates it behind a signup. Here are both branches, in full, no email required.


### When you're not ready to demo yet


> "Happy to show you exactly this. So I don't waste your time on the wrong screens, give me two minutes: what's the workflow that made you take this call? I'll pull up that piece specifically and send you a guided version to keep after."


That sets up the leave-behind, which matters because, as one leader put it bluntly, nobody re-watches a recording.


> "the reality is, is nobody's watching a follow-up recording of a demo; that just doesn't happen."
>
>
> - \[Solutions Engineering manager, restaurant management software\]


### When you can demo on the spot


> "Let's do it. I'm going to show you the one workflow that fixes what you just described, then I'll pause and you tell me if I nailed it or missed. Everything else, I'll send as a guided walkthrough you can click through on your own time."


It still protects discovery by asking them to react: you demo the diagnosed problem, confirm the read, and route the rest to a leave-behind.


## Common Mistakes That Derail a Combined Discovery-Demo Call


Most combined calls fail for the same handful of reasons, and each has a one-line fix.


- **Demoing the whole product because discovery was thin.** If you cannot name the one workflow to show, you are not ready, so tease and follow up.
- **Confusing "complex product" with "complex demo."** Buyers call a product complex right after asking complex questions, so simplify the path you show, not the product. One principal SE named the contradiction: "The other side of it, too, is people say that it's really complex after they just spent 30 minutes asking really complex questions." - \[principal sales engineer, restaurant management software\]
- **Falling back on a recording nobody watches.** Send a guided, click-through leave-behind that lets the buyer re-walk the exact path.
- **Handing over a raw, unguided sandbox too early.** Use a guided demo for first touches and reserve open sandboxes for late-stage, hands-on evaluation.
- **Building every live demo from scratch.** Pre-build teaser tours by persona so "demo now" does not mean "improvise now."


## How Interactive Demos Remove the Discovery-vs-Demo Tradeoff


Full disclosure: this is us. Storylane Demo Suite exists because the discovery-vs-demo tradeoff is mostly an artifact of demos being expensive to prepare. When a tailored demo takes a specialist a day to build, reps hoard them for big deals and default to generic tours elsewhere.


The mechanism is simple: build guided, interactive demos once, then reuse and tailor them per call. It also fixes a real operational tax our buyers described, like the SE who ran a Parallels license and a local server on his laptop just to bring up one product.


Where Demo Suite does not fit is the low-cost transactional sale, where buyers convert self-serve and a short generic tour beats a custom build. It does not replace discovery either; it just makes the demo half cheap enough to stop rationing.


### Pre-built teaser tours by use case and persona


Curate a small library of guided tours, one per persona and top use case, so any rep can show the right thing without an SE on the call. One buyer described this exact "master hub" motion: keep a full menu, then clone and curate a version per prospect.


Data matters too, so a coffee chain should not see a seafood brand's reporting, and you build the reusable base once with[an interactive product demo](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-create-an-interactive-product-demo) .


### Configuring a tailored tour live, based on what you just heard in discovery


The true gap no competitor closes is doing this in the call. You finish discovery, clone a base tour, swap in the prospect's vertical and priority, and show it minutes later.


That turns "just show me a demo" into a tailored moment, and it is the heart of[micro-demos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/micro-demos) . Buyers notice: one VP evaluating options told us, "Just looking at those two Storylane looks simpler, I would say. Like it's more straightforward." - \[VP of Marketing, education / yearbook publishing\]


## FAQs


**How long should a discovery call be?**


Most B2B discovery calls run 30 to 45 minutes, long enough to diagnose the problem. If a buyer wants to see the product, do not burn it all on questions; earn two or three answers, then transition into a short teaser.


**Should SDRs ever demo, or only AEs?**


SDRs can show a short, pre-built guided demo to confirm interest, but they should not run a full custom demo. That work belongs to an AE or SE who can read the room, so arm SDRs with reusable teaser tours instead.


**What if the person on the call isn't the actual decision-maker?**


Demo lightly, then equip your contact to sell internally. A guided, click-through leave-behind travels to the real decision-maker far better than a recording.


**Does the answer change for enterprise vs. SMB deals?**


Yes. For smaller deals, a guided leave-behind usually beats a live custom demo on time spent per outcome. For enterprise deals with multiple stakeholders, a tailored live demo is worth the effort.


**What's the difference between teasing a demo and running a full demo?**


A teaser shows one workflow tied to the buyer's top priority, then defers the rest. A full demo covers the product broadly and risks comprehension loss, so on a combined discovery call you almost always want the teaser.
